In addition to this, risks of hypoglycemic state and resulting side effects limit their use, for example, insulin, sulfonylureas, and glitazones increase IR by facilitating weight gain and pioglitazone causes edema, cardiovascular difficulties (Clar et al., 2012, p. Increasingly, studies are addressing the effects of different classes of chalcones on glycemic modulation through serum glucose lowering, activation of GLUT-4 translocation, glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and/or insulin secretion, applying both *in vivo* as *in vitro* procedures. Additionally, the effect of the chalcones studied on insulin secretion and serum glucose lowering was similar to that of glipizide. This report indicates that the effect of chalcones on serum glucose lowering in hyperglycemic-normal rats is mainly a consequence of insulin secretion, highlighting these chalcones as novel compounds with strong antihyperglycemic properties [4]. As the effects of the SGLT2 inhibitors are directed specifically to enhancing glucosuria, it appears that the reduction of metabolic load reduces glucose toxicity and is disease-modifying, which drives other positive effects such as reduced insulin levels, increased beta cell insulin content, improved insulin sensitivity, and enhanced postprandial glucose disposal.94 Additional therapeutic interventions such as insulin or insulin secretagogues increase the possibility of hypoglycemia, and increased vigilance for possible euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis needs to be managed moving forward. In a recent publication from Takano and Toda et al., the optimizations of 3-aryl-3-ethoxypropanoic acids were performed leading to the identification of a new agent **DS-1558**, (3*S*)-3-ethoxy-3-(4-{[(1*R*)-4-(trifluoromethyl)-2,3-dihydro-1*H*-inden-1-yl]oxy}phenyl)propanoic acid, which had efficacy on glucose-dependent insulin secretion after intravenous glucose injection in SD rats.232 Notably, an induced-fit docking study of **DS-1558** was carried out using the X-ray structure of GPR40, in which the molecule docked very well to the same binding site with a slightly rotated side chain of Trp174.

results.title: CGM for Insulin Resistance: A Closer Look at Glycemic Trends
results.content: Published Time: 2025-04-29T19:29:55+00:00 CGM for Insulin Resistance: A Closer Look at Glycemic Trends - BiologyInsights #### Account CGM for Insulin Resistance: A Closer Look at Glycemic Trends Explore how continuous glucose monitoring provides insight into glycemic patterns, helping to better understand and manage insulin resistance over time. Tracking glucose levels continuously has become a key tool for managing insulin resistance. Unlike traditional fingerstick tests, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides real-time data on fluctuations throughout the day, offering insights into how diet, activity, and other factors affect blood sugar levels. Glucose Patterns In Insulin Resistance Individuals with insulin resistance often experience distinct glucose fluctuations. A study in Diabetes Care (2021) found that those with insulin resistance had a median postprandial glucose peak of 160–180 mg/dL, compared to 120–140 mg/dL in individuals with normal insulin function. Fasting glucose levels in insulin resistance also tend to be elevated, even if they fall within the “normal” range. Mechanisms Of Sensor-Based Glucose Measurement CGM relies on sensor-based technology to track glucose levels in real time. This distinction is particularly relevant for individuals with insulin resistance, where glucose excursions can be more pronounced and prolonged. This continuous data stream allows individuals to recognize delayed postprandial glucose clearance and heightened glycemic variability—two hallmarks of insulin resistance that are often missed with intermittent testing. The sensor continuously measures glucose levels and transmits data to a receiver or smartphone. For individuals with insulin resistance, these devices provide valuable insights into postprandial glucose responses and nocturnal fluctuations, helping refine dietary and exercise strategies. For individuals with insulin resistance, long-term monitoring can help track gradual changes in glucose regulation, offering a broader view of metabolic trends. Once in place, the sensor continuously measures glucose levels, with data accessed via a smartphone or reader. For individuals managing insulin resistance, patch systems provide a convenient way to track glucose trends without frequent interventions, supporting more informed lifestyle adjustments. Observing Glycemic Trends In Insulin Resistance CGM provides a dynamic view of glucose fluctuations, revealing patterns that traditional testing often misses. While glucose levels in individuals with normal insulin sensitivity typically peak within 30–60 minutes post-meal and return to fasting levels within two hours, those with insulin resistance experience prolonged elevations.

results.title: Tandem Mobi Insulin Pump Now Compatible with Dexcom G7 CGM
results.content: Tandem Mobi Insulin Pump Now Compatible with Dexcom G7 CGM. **Tandem Mobi Insulin Pump Now Compatible with Dexcom G7 CGM**. Tandem Mobi insulin pump from Tandem Diabetes Care is now compatible with Dexcom G7 Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) System. (Nasdaq: DXCM), today announced that the Tandem Mobi insulin pump with Control-IQ technology is now fully compatible with both the Dexcom G7 and Dexcom G6 Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) Systems. Tandem is now the only company that offers people living with diabetes two insulin pump options that connect with both Dexcom G6 and Dexcom G7, providing more choice in how they manage their diabetes. Powered by Control-IQ technology, which has demonstrated in real-world studies improved time in range overnight and during the day4, Tandem Mobi connects with Dexcom G7 or Dexcom G6 to predict glucose levels 30 minutes in advance and automatically adjusts insulin, if needed, to help prevent highs and lows. “We are proud to offer people with diabetes the ability to use Dexcom G7, our smallest and most accurate CGM, with Tandem Mobi to create a seamless user experience.”. 4. All published clinical trials and real-world studies of Control-IQ technology to date are based on use of Dexcom G6 CGM with the Tandem t:slim X2 insulin pump. The Company’s pump portfolio features the Tandem Mobi system and the t:slim X2 insulin pump, both of which feature Control-IQ advanced hybrid closed-loop technology. Tandem Diabetes Care, the Tandem logo, Control-IQ, t:slim X2, and Tandem Mobi are either registered trademarks or trademarks of Tandem Diabetes Care, Inc. in the United States and/or other countries. Indications for Use: Tandem Mobi system: The Tandem Mobi insulin pump with interoperable technology (the pump) is intended for the subcutaneous delivery of insulin, at set and variable rates, for the management of diabetes mellitus in persons requiring insulin. Users of a Tandem insulin pump and Control-IQ technology must use the insulin pump, CGM, and all other system components in accordance with their respective instructions for use; test blood glucose levels as recommended by their healthcare provider; demonstrate adequate carb-counting skills; maintain sufficient diabetes self-care skills; see healthcare provider(s) regularly; and have adequate vision and/or hearing to recognize all functions of the pump, including alerts, alarms, and reminders.

results.title: FDA Panel Votes YES to Using Dexcom’s G5 CGM for Insulin Dosing | DiaTribe
results.content:
Title: FDA Panel Votes YES to Using Dexcom’s G5 CGM for Insulin Dosing | DiaTribe
# FDA Panel Votes YES to Using Dexcom’s G5 CGM for Insulin Dosing. *An 8-2 panel vote finds that benefits of using Dexcom’s G5 CGM for dosing insulin outweigh the risks; patient advocates provide compelling testimonies*. On July 21, an advisory panel strongly recommended that the FDA approve a label update allowing Dexcom’s G5 CGM (continuous glucose monitor) to be used for making diabetes treatment decisions (e.g., insulin dosing) without a confirmation fingerstick. risk tradeoffs of this label update very positively, and patients and healthcare providers made a particularly strong impact – ensuring that the panel focused away from theoretical points that don’t have too much to do with “real life” diabetes. * Allow healthcare providers to formally educate users on proper insulin dosing using Dexcom’s G5 CGM (many people dose with CGM already, but don’t receive any education to do it as safely as possible). During the Open Public Hearing, over 35 patient advocates, including people with diabetes (adults, children, and teens), family members, healthcare providers, diabetes researchers, and professional organizations (JDRF, AACE, ADA, and the Endocrine Society) provided compelling commentary on why this label update will benefit people with diabetes:. * Dexcom G5 CGM users widely use it for insulin dosing already, meaning this label update simply reflects real-world practice. Additionally, proper education – for people with diabetes and for healthcare providers – can’t occur without an approved label update. Instead of receiving structured guidance and training, people with diabetes are currently learning how to use CGM for insulin dosing via trial and error. Assuming the update is approved, Dexcom will be able to teach when NOT to use CGM for insulin dosing – for example, when a trend arrow doesn’t appear, when there are gaps in data, when symptoms don’t match the CGM readings, etc. * “Approving this label will keep people with diabetes safer and allow proper education for those who are dosing off CGM now from trial and error.” – Adam Brown (The diaTribe Foundation). We were excited to amplify patient voice and help the FDA understand why this label update matters to people with diabetes.
